title: The King Who Tried to Prove Coffee Was Poison
sources: Swedish National Archives, 'Gustav III's coffee experiment' (King Adolf Frederick issued royal decrees against coffee in 1746; Gustav III conducted the clinical trial on twin prisoners condemned to death)
Mark Pendergrast, 'Uncommon Grounds: The History of Coffee and How It Transformed Our World'
The Lancet / medical histories of early Swedish clinical trials

lines.text: In seventeen forty-six, the King of Sweden decided coffee was a deadly poison,
so he banned every single cup in the country.
When citizens kept brewing it in secret,
he launched the weirdest royal experiment in history.
He found two identical twin prisoners on death row,
and offered them a strange royal pardon:
as long as one drank three pots of coffee every day,
while his brother drank three pots of tea.
Two royal doctors were ordered to watch them closely,
waiting for the coffee drinker to drop dead.
Except... both doctors died of old age first.
Then the King himself was assassinated.
Decades later, the tea drinker passed away at eighty-three,

lines.text: leaving the coffee drinker alive, happily sipping his daily brew.
